chunks: "Saturation current matters because an inductor only stores energy while its core can take more flux.
Once the current pushes the core to its saturation flux density, the inductance collapses.
Since the inductor current slope is V over L , a collapsed L means the current shoots up with almost nothing to limit it except the resistance and the controller's reaction time.
That can overshoot the current limit, stress the FETs, increase ripple and EMI, and in a short circuit ratchet the current until something breaks.
So I choose the inductor's saturation current above the IC's maximum current limit, with margin for temperature, since ferrite saturates at lower current when hot, and for the tolerance on the limit.
The load current plus half ripple is not enough. DCR versus ACR: DCR is the copper resistance, which sets I to the 2R loss at full load.
ACR is the effective resistance at the switching frequency, where skin and proximity effects and core loss add loss to the ripple component.
At heavy load DCR dominates; at light load or high frequency with big ripple, ACR and core loss can dominate, so a low-DCR inductor can still be a hot, inefficient one."
